title: Prefixes and suffixes: how they help spelling
meta_description: Prefixes and suffixes follow a few rules that children meet from Year 1 to Year 6. Here is what the national curriculum says, and how to help at home.
hero_image_alt: A closed navy notebook, a navy pencil and a pink eraser on a pale wooden table, with a mug of tea beside a blank ruled notepad.
content_html:
Prefixes and suffixes are word parts added to the front or end of a root word, and they matter for spelling because they follow rules. A child who knows that the root keeps its spelling, and who knows the few rules that change it when an ending is added, has far fewer words to learn one at a time.

Key takeaways

  • The national curriculum spelling appendix says pupils can be helped to spell words with prefixes and suffixes correctly if they understand some general principles for adding them.
  • Most suffix changes come down to four patterns: add the ending as it is, drop a final e, change y to i, or double the last consonant.
  • Children meet these patterns gradually from Year 1 to Year 6, with the rules revised at the start of each stage before new endings are added.
  • A 2010 review identified twenty two studies of morphological instruction and found that it benefits learners, with particular benefits for less able readers.
  • At home, the most useful habit is to ask which part of a misspelt word is the root and which part is the ending, then use look, cover, write, check on the whole word.

What are prefixes and suffixes?

A prefix is a group of letters added to the start of a root word, and a suffix is a group of letters added to the end. That is the ordinary grammar definition rather than a quotation: the spelling appendix uses both terms throughout but never defines them. The root word is the part that carries the main meaning, and the prefix or suffix changes or extends it.

Children usually meet the idea through familiar examples. The appendix notes that the prefix un is added to the beginning of a word without any change to the spelling of the root, and that the suffix ly is added to an adjective to form an adverb. The endings ing and ed change the tense of a verb.

Why do prefixes and suffixes matter for spelling?

Prefixes and suffixes matter for spelling because their rules let a child spell many words from one known root, instead of treating each long word as a new puzzle. The Department for Education's spelling appendix says: “Pupils can also be helped to spell words with prefixes and suffixes correctly.” It attaches that to understanding some general principles for adding them.

The appendix also says children increasingly need to understand the role of morphology and etymology. Morphology is how words are built from parts. Etymology is where words come from. In the notes for Years 3 and 4 it works the idea through: the root word appear contains sounds that can be spelt in more than one way, so it has to be learnt, but the prefix dis is then simply added to it. It explains bicycle as cycle, from the Greek for wheel, with bi, meaning two, before it.

The same appendix is clear that the knowledge has limits. It says that particular sound and letter matches in root words simply have to be learnt. Word parts help with what is added to a root. They do not remove the need to learn the root itself.

Does a prefix change the spelling of the root word?

Most prefixes are added to the beginning of root words without any change in spelling, which the appendix states directly. That is why the appear in disappear is spelt exactly as it is on its own.

This is the most useful fact for a parent to share with a child, because it turns a long word into two short ones.

What happens to a root word when a suffix is added?

The appendix describes a small set of ways a root word changes when a suffix is added, and most endings fall into one of them. Each rule below is stated in the appendix. The examples in the table are illustrations written for this post, not quotations from it.

PatternWhat happensIllustration
Add the ending as it isIf a verb ends in two consonant letters, the ending is simply addedwalk, walking
Drop the final eThe e at the end of the root word is dropped before an ending that begins with a vowel lettermake, making
Change y to iThe y is changed to i before ed, er and est are added, but not before ing. A separate rule changes y to i before escry, cried, crying
Double the last consonantThe last consonant is doubled to keep the vowel shorthop, hopping

The appendix also lists exceptions, and it is better to know they exist than to hide them. It says the letter x is never doubled, giving mixing, mixed, boxer and sixes. For longer words, the consonant letter is not doubled if the syllable is unstressed. And being is listed as an exception to dropping the e.

The suffixes ment, ness, ful, less and ly are generally added straight onto the root, with exceptions the appendix lists. For ly, those include roots ending in y after a consonant with more than one syllable, where the y changes to i. The appendix also lists truly, duly and wholly as exceptions in their own right.

When do children learn these rules at school?

Children learn prefix and suffix rules in stages across Years 1 to 6, and each stage begins by revising the rules from the one before. In Year 1, children add simple endings where the root does not change, and meet the prefix un. In Year 2, they learn the rules that change the root, dropping e, changing y to i and doubling, along with endings such as ment, ness, ful, less and ly.

In Years 3 and 4, the appendix begins with revision and then extends the rules to longer words, where stress decides whether a consonant is doubled. Further prefixes and endings are introduced. In Years 5 and 6, revision comes first again, followed by further endings including the pairs able and ible, and ance and ence.

The appendix also tells teachers to be familiar with what pupils have been taught earlier. For a parent, the practical meaning may be that a child struggling with a Year 4 ending is missing an earlier rule rather than the new one.

Is any of this compulsory?

The appendix is part of the statutory national curriculum, but not every column in it is. It states that the left hand column is statutory and the middle and right hand columns are non statutory guidance, and that the word lists for Years 3 and 4 and for Years 5 and 6 are statutory. The Department for Education's page states that all schools maintained by the local authority in England must teach the programmes of study. The page does not set out the position for other types of school, so this post makes no claim about them.

What does research say about teaching word parts?

A review published in 2010 by Bowers, Kirby and Deacon identified twenty two peer reviewed studies of morphological instruction, with participants from preschool to Grade 8. Its abstract reports that the instruction benefits learners, that it brings particular benefits for less able readers, that it is no less effective for younger students, and that it is more effective when combined with other aspects of literacy instruction.

That is a narrower finding than it first appears. The authors investigated effects on reading, spelling, vocabulary and morphological skills together, and the abstract reports no result for spelling on its own, so nothing here shows that teaching word parts improves spelling specifically. The review is about teaching in schools, not practice at home, and it says nothing about any particular app.

How can a parent help at home?

The most useful help is to split a misspelt word into root and ending, because that shows the child where the error sits. That follows from the appendix rules above rather than from any study of parents at home.

A routine might run in four short steps. First, ask the child to point to the root word. Second, ask which prefix or suffix has been added. Third, ask whether a rule changed the root, such as a dropped e or a changed y. Fourth, use look, cover, write, check on the whole word, covering it and writing it from memory so that the child is not copying.

The covering step matters because recognising a rule is not the same as spelling a word from memory. The page on how spelling sticks sets out how practice that involves recall fits into learning a word. For a wider view of why English spelling has so many exceptions, see why English spelling is so hard to learn.

FAQ

Do all prefixes and suffixes follow a rule?

No. The appendix lists exceptions beside most of its rules, including being for dropping e, and truly, duly and wholly for the ly ending. A child can use the rules as a starting point and learn the exceptions as individual words.

What is the difference between a root word and a prefix?

A root word is the part that carries the main meaning, and a prefix is added to its front to change or extend that meaning. That is the ordinary grammar definition; the spelling appendix uses the terms but does not define them.

Should a child learn the rules before the weekly list?

The appendix does not say which should come first. A child who has met the rule in class will find the list easier, and a child who finds the list hard can be shown the rule behind the words. Ask the class teacher which rule the list is built on.

Are patterns such as ough prefixes or suffixes?

No. The appendix treats them as spelling patterns and lists them separately from prefixes and suffixes. They are learnt as patterns, not built from word parts.

If your child practises weekly lists at home, Spelling Nest keeps the same look, cover, write, check method and adds a short daily game alongside the writing.
